notes: Court of Appeal (Jonathan Parker, Charles and Potter LJJ); Revenue appeal on Caudwell Group employee benefit trust contributions.

enrichment.short_title: Employee benefit trust contributions as potential emoluments
key_facts: Six Caudwell Group companies made substantial December 1998 contributions to a Jersey employee benefit trust with an independent trustee.
The companies sought Schedule D deductions for the contributions; the Inspector disallowed them as potential emoluments under section 43(11).
Special Commissioners and Neuberger J upheld the companies, construing potential emoluments as requiring a dominant purpose of providing emoluments.
The trust permitted wide discretionary benefits including interest-free loans that were not emoluments.
The Revenue appealed on the construction of amounts held by an intermediary with a view to becoming relevant emoluments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on a second appeal from the Special Commissioners via the High Court, limited to section 43 Finance Act 1989.
enrichment.outcome: Revenue appeal allowed; contributions held to be potential emoluments postponing deductibility.
enrichment.ratio: For section 43(11)(a) Finance Act 1989, where contributions are held by a trustee under a genuine discretionary settlement, whether they are potential emoluments depends primarily on the terms on which the funds are held; if realistic outcomes under the trust include non-emolument benefits, the flexible phrase with a view to their becoming relevant emoluments embraces those possibilities and deferral applies even where some funds may never become deductible emoluments.
legal_issues: Meaning of potential emoluments and with a view to in section 43(11)(a)
Whether the contributing company's purpose or the trustee's holding terms govern classification
Application of section 43 to employee benefit trusts and interest-free loans
Fiscal symmetry between employer deductions and employee receipts

notes: Family contact appeal; Butler-Sloss P with Thorpe and Carnwath LJJ.

enrichment.short_title: Father's appeal against refusal of direct contact
key_facts: A six-year-old girl had enjoyed good contact with her father until parental hostility escalated after May 2001.
Multiple CAFCASS reports and supervised contact sessions failed; the child became entrenched in opposition to contact.
The recorder dismissed direct contact, ordered indirect contact unlikely to work, refused a psychological assessment, and imposed a one-year section 91(14) bar.
The recorder found the mother primarily responsible for obstructing contact but effectively closed the door on future direct contact.
The Court of Appeal considered extensive guidance on contact, domestic violence, and section 91(14) restrictions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a recorder's contact order following prolonged county court proceedings and stale CAFCASS evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: joint psychiatric assessment ordered, case restored to a circuit judge, and section 91(14) order set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Courts should not prematurely abandon attempts to restore contact between a genuinely motivated non-resident parent and a young child where the primary carer has undermined contact; a broad family assessment may be required before closing the door, and section 91(14) is a draconian discretionary power requiring proportionality and evidence of unacceptable strain.
legal_issues: When refusal of direct contact is premature despite entrenched parental conflict
Appropriate use of expert psychiatric assessment in contact disputes
Lawfulness and proportionality of section 91(14) Children Act orders
Balancing Article 8 rights with the child's welfare as paramount

notes: Reserved reasons on joint enterprise appeal; Mantell LJ; Uddin and Alamin Miah convictions quashed.

enrichment.short_title: Unsafe joint enterprise convictions after DLR attack
key_facts: Following a New Year's Eve 2001 attack on Philip Bowden on the Docklands Light Railway, three defendants were convicted of GBH with intent or violent disorder.
CCTV showed the appellants in the group but eyewitnesses could not identify participants in the stabbing and beating.
The Crown case depended on prior agreement by all who alighted to attack the victim, formulated as joint enterprise.
Five co-defendants were acquitted, undermining the proposition that every group member shared the agreed purpose.
The court had already allowed Uddin and Alamin Miah's appeals at a hearing before giving reserved reasons.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) giving reserved reasons after allowing appeals against conviction on no-case and jury inconsistency grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals of Maruf Uddin and Alamin Miah allowed; convictions on counts 1 and 2 respectively quashed as unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: Where not every group member participated and the jury acquitted others, convictions for causing GBH with intent cannot safely rest on inferred prior agreement that all members intended serious harm before alighting; and if the jury rejected joint enterprise on violent disorder for acquitted co-defendants, there was no basis to convict remaining appellants on that count either.
legal_issues: Sufficiency of evidence for joint enterprise GBH with intent
Inference of shared intent to cause serious harm before the attack
Effect of partial acquittals on remaining joint enterprise convictions
Whether violent disorder count should have been left to the jury

notes: Supplemental quantum judgment only; Cooke J following 28 January 2004 Lloyd's Names decision; decimal-point error corrected.

enrichment.short_title: Lloyd's Name Drysdale counterclaim quantum on statutory demand
key_facts: Following an earlier judgment on Lloyd's Names amendment applications, Cooke J invited further submissions on Mr Drysdale's arguable loss quantum.
Drysdale's revised figures corrected a misplaced decimal point in syndicate 89 calculations for the 1982 underwriting year.
Closed-year profit and open syndicate 126, 700 and 89 figures were reconciled against Lloyd's publicly available accounts.
Even on the most generous assessment for Drysdale, his maximum aggregate 1982 loss claim was about £39,425.
His latest calculation of £30,436 could not equal or exceed the statutory demand figure of £310,504.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplementary Commercial Court judgment on quantum after an earlier interlocutory Lloyd's Names decision.
enrichment.outcome: Drysdale's counterclaim could not arguably equal or exceed the statutory demand amount.
enrichment.ratio: Once corrected underwriting figures for the 1982 year are applied on the principles already determined, the Name's maximum arguable aggregate loss remains far below the Equitas premium-based statutory demand and cannot defeat it on quantum.
legal_issues: Calculation of a Lloyd's Name's 1982 underwriting loss across closed and open syndicates
Effect of decimal error in syndicate 89 loss calculations
Whether counterclaim quantum could equal a bankruptcy statutory demand

notes: Sentencing and confiscation appeal; Poole J with VP and judge; large-scale counterfeit US dollar conspiracy.

enrichment.short_title: Counterfeit currency sentencing and confiscation evidence rules
key_facts: Silcock and Levin were sentenced for conspiring to import and distribute high-quality counterfeit US $100 notes linked to organised crime.
Levin received nine years concurrent on two counts and a confiscation order of about £789,300 plus interest.
At confiscation the judge relied on trial evidence, prosecution statements, and witness statements not tested at trial.
Levin appealed on manifest excess of sentence and admissibility/weight of hearsay in confiscation proceedings.
Silcock appealed sentence disparity and credit for his late guilty plea.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) appeals against sentence and confiscation order after a long Crown Court trial and confiscation hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; sentences upheld and confiscation order confirmed.
enrichment.ratio: Following the 1993 amendments to the Criminal Justice Act 1988, confiscation proceedings use the civil standard of proof and may rely on relevant information and untested witness material when determining benefit and realisable assets, provided the judge scrutinises weight carefully; pre-1993 drug-trafficking authority on admissible evidence does not govern the amended regime.
legal_issues: Whether ordinary criminal evidence rules apply in confiscation hearings
Appropriate sentences for large-scale international counterfeit currency conspiracies
Use of co-defendant interview admissions and untested witness statements at confiscation
Disparity between co-conspirators' sentences

notes: Detailed assessment under Solicitors Act 1974; Costs Judge Ian Donaldson; modest probate estate.

enrichment.short_title: Beneficiary's challenge to probate solicitors' bills
key_facts: The residuary beneficiary challenged solicitors' bills totalling £26,108.88 for administering an estate worth about £279,000.
A deputy district judge ordered detailed assessment within the twelve-month Solicitors Act period.
The beneficiary was not the solicitors' client or an entitled third party under the 1994 Remuneration Order because a lay executor was involved.
Correspondence with the beneficiary did not make her a quasi-client despite her strong interest in estate costs.
Applying Jemma Trust v Liptrott guidance, the costs judge found the overall charge fair and reasonable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Detailed assessment in the Supreme Court Costs Office after transfer from Colchester District Registry.
enrichment.outcome: Bills assessed as delivered with no reduction; claimant ordered to pay defendants' costs of £7,500.
enrichment.ratio: A residuary beneficiary who is not the solicitors' client or an entitled third party under the Remuneration Order may still apply for assessment under the Solicitors Act, but the ultimate test remains whether the total charge is fair and reasonable in all the circumstances under the Remuneration Order and Court of Appeal guidance.
legal_issues: Who qualifies as client or entitled third party for probate bill assessment
Whether a beneficiary can be treated as a quasi-client from correspondence
Application of Jemma Trust v Liptrott to overall fair and reasonable remuneration
Costs consequences where less than 20% of bills is reduced

notes: Very long trial judgment; Langley J; damages base £10.2m subject to party adjustment per expert figures.

enrichment.short_title: Exclusive Shoprider scooter distribution agreement repudiation
key_facts: Days Medical Aids held a five-year exclusive UK and mainland Europe distribution agreement for Pihsiang Shoprider mobility scooters from February 1996.
DMA paid substantial upfront fees and renewed in February 2001 after meeting sales and performance conditions.
Pihsiang began supplying other European distributors from November 2000; DMA accepted repudiation in April 2002.
Mr and Mrs Wu personally undertook Pihsiang's obligations under the agreement.
The court found valid renewal, repudiatory breach, and damages based primarily on expert loss figures for the ten-year term ending February 2006.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Commercial Court trial of breach, renewal, restraint of trade, Article 81, and quantification of claim and counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Claim largely succeeded: agreement treated as a ten-year contract; DMA entitled to substantial damages for repudiation; counterclaim dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a distributor validly renews an exclusive distribution agreement by meeting Clause 10 conditions and the manufacturer repudiates by appointing competing distributors, the distributor may recover loss of bargain damages for the remaining contractual term; unlimited renewal clauses may engage restraint of trade but Article 81 can preserve enforceability, and future renewals beyond the first renewal period involve heavily discounted speculative loss.
legal_issues: Construction of renewal conditions including discharged its obligations and 5000-unit sales threshold
Personal liability of Mr and Mrs Wu and non est factum
Whether the agreement was void for restraint of trade or saved by EC law
Article 81 analysis and block exemption application
Assessment of loss of profits and mitigation through alternative suppliers

notes: Administrative Court judicial review; Mitting J; Hindawi and Headley parole challenges.

enrichment.short_title: Article 14 challenge to deportee parole procedure
key_facts: Two long-term prisoners subject to deportation orders challenged refusal of early release on licence.
Section 46 CJA 1991 removes the Parole Board recommendation requirement for prisoners liable to removal.
The Home Secretary refused release without Board review; Hindawi also argued inadequate reasons ignoring changed conditions in Syria.
Claimants argued Article 14 discrimination compared with non-deportable prisoners serving similar sentences.
Carlisle Committee reasoning for a separate deportee framework was relied on but not reconciled with other parole regimes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of Home Secretary parole decisions for deportable long-term prisoners.
enrichment.outcome: Applications granted; parole refusal decisions quashed for unlawful Article 14 discrimination and, in Hindawi's case, inadequate reasons.
enrichment.ratio: Early release provisions for deportable long-term prisoners engage Article 5 and Article 14; denying them Parole Board review while granting it to comparable non-deportable prisoners is differential treatment without adequate objective justification, and a refusal letter must address the principal issue raised, including foreign-policy-based risk arguments.
legal_issues: Whether parole legislation falls within the ambit of Article 5 for Article 14 purposes
Objective justification for excluding deportable prisoners from Parole Board review
Whether discrimination is based on nationality or liability to removal
Adequacy of reasons where expert evidence on country conditions is ignored

notes: Election petition appeal; Tuckey, Sedley and Wall LJJ; Dudley local election postal votes.

enrichment.short_title: Meaning of issue to in postal ballot rules

statutes_considered.title: Representation of the People (England and Wales) Regulations 2001

key_facts: An election petition challenged a Dudley ward result where postal votes may have decided the forty-vote margin.
597 postal ballot packs were issued via Royal Mail; over 110 voters received papers late or after polling day despite replacement procedures.
The returning officer complied with regulations including Regulation 78 replacement ballot provisions.
The Divisional Court held issue to did not require personal delivery to each postal voter.
The petitioner argued strict delivery obligations and Article 3 First Protocol implications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on a special case from an election petition under section 146 Representation of the People Act 1983.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; election not invalidated under section 48.
enrichment.ratio: In rule 19 LEPAR and the 2001 postal ballot regulations, issue to a postal voter means properly addressing and sending the ballot to an authorised carrier for delivery, not guaranteeing receipt in the voter's hands; Regulation 78 provides the safety net and non-delivery by the carrier does not invalidate the election where the returning officer took appropriate steps.
legal_issues: Construction of issue to in LEPAR rule 19
Returning officer's duties when Royal Mail fails to deliver postal ballots
Interaction of Regulation 76 delivery and Regulation 78 replacement ballots
Whether section 48 permits invalidating an election for late postal votes

notes: Fresh evidence appeal; Thomas LJ; conviction safe despite Heidi Merryweather witness.

enrichment.short_title: Rape conviction appeal and fresh witness evidence
key_facts: The appellant was convicted of raping acquaintance A after partial penetration at her flat in September 2001.
He was acquitted on two other rape counts involving different complainants.
On appeal he sought to adduce fresh evidence from Heidi Merryweather about post-incident conversations.
Defence solicitors failed to contact Merryweather before trial despite knowing her address and tactical reasons for not seeking CPS help.
The court found her appeal evidence inconsistent and incapable of belief; sentence was reduced from six to five years and costs orders quashed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on fresh evidence under section 23 and sentence/costs appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed; sentence reduced to five years; prosecution and defence costs orders set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh evidence will not be received under section 23 where there is no reasonable explanation for its absence at trial and the evidence is incapable of belief by any jury; tactical refusal to ask the CPS to trace a known witness is not a reasonable explanation, and a rape sentence may be reduced where penetration was brief and there were no aggravating features beyond harm to the victim.
legal_issues: Section 23 criteria for admitting fresh evidence on appeal
Reasonableness of defence failure to call a known witness before trial
Credibility of inconsistent post-conviction witness accounts
Appropriate sentence and costs orders where means were not investigated
linked_authorities: R v Pendleton [2001] UKHL 66
R v Milberry [2003] 2 Cr App R (S)
